titre: Graphics: the screen, bitplanes and the palette
resume: The Atari's screen is an area of memory where, in low resolution, each pixel is made of four bits spread over four **interleaved bitplanes**. You compute the address of a pixel there, fix the manual's PSET routine, which contains two errors, and change the colors of the whole screen through the palette. Module 3 of the Atari ST manual and exercises 7.1-1 and 7.2 of its module 7.

atari-ch05-rappel.introduction: Three questions on the previous chapters, without rereading the lessons. Getting it wrong here does not matter: searching is what makes it stick.

q1.explication: The counter starts at 2, so DBRA goes round 3 times, and D3 goes from 'A' to 'C'.

q2.enonce: Why does the program count the rounds in D4 rather than in D1?
choix: Because TOS may modify D0-D2 during a call
Because DBRA does not accept D1
Out of habit: D1 would work too
q2.explication: TOS preserves D3-D7 and A3-A6, but may modify D0-D2 and A0-A2: a counter in D1 could be damaged by the TRAP.

q3.enonce: Started in user mode, could this program write directly to `$FF8240`?
choix: Yes, as to any memory location
q3.explication: The hardware registers are protected in user mode: you have to go through Supexec, or through a function such as Setcolor.

atari-ch05-cours-ecran.source: Rephrased from the Atari ST manual v1 (§ 3.1-3.3) and v2 (§ 3.1-3.3), formulas corrected (see the errata of the manual v2)

atari-ch05-ex-pixel.titre: Turning on a pixel, step by step
atari-ch05-ex-pixel.introduction: The program turns on the pixel (37, 100) in color 1: follow the computation of the address in A0, then look at the screen in the right-hand panel, where a small red dot appears halfway down, on the left.

explications.4: Physbase has returned the address of the screen in D0, `$000F8000`.
explications.5: A0 points to the first byte of the screen, at the top left.
explications.7: 100 × 160 = 16,000 bytes separate the start of the screen from the start of line 100.
explications.8: A0 now points to the start of line 100, `$FBE80`.
explications.11: 37 ÷ 16 = 2 in integer division: the pixel is in the 3rd group of 16 pixels.
explications.12: Each group takes up 8 bytes, which gives an offset of 16 bytes.
explications.13: A0 points to plane 0 of the group that holds pixels 32 to 47.
explications.14: 37 mod 16 = 5: it is the 6th pixel of the group.
explications.16: Since the leftmost pixel is bit 15, the 6th one is bit 15 − 5 = 10.
explications.18: D5 becomes a mask in which only bit 10 is 1, `%0000 0100 0000 0000`.
explications.19: OR turns this bit on in plane 0 without touching the other 15 pixels of the word: the pixel takes color %0001 = 1, red with the default palette.

atari-ch05-ex-pixel.conclusion: The pixel (X, Y) is in the word at screen + Y × 160 + (X ÷ 16) × 8, at bit 15 − (X mod 16), and every graphics routine on the ST relies on this computation.

atari-ch05-pred-adresse.introduction: This is exercise 1 of module 7 of the manual: with the screen of a 1040 ST at `$F8000`, where is the group that holds the pixel (160, 100)? Devpac, like vasm, computes the expression at assembly time.

q2.enonce: And D2, the number of the pixel's bit in its word?
q2.explication: 160 mod 16 = 0: it is the first pixel of the group, the one at bit 15.

atari-ch05-exo-couleur3.enonce: The program turns on the pixel (0, 0) in plane 0. Add one instruction so that it takes color 3 (`%0011`).
indices: Color 3 has its bits 0 and 1 at 1: planes 0 and 1.

atari-ch05-exo-ligne.enonce: On line Y = 10, draw a 32-pixel stroke, from X = 0 to X = 31, in color 1.
indices: The start of line 10 is at screen + 10 × 160 (`LEA 10*160(A0),A0`).
32 pixels make 2 groups, and plane 0 of the 2nd group is 8 bytes further on.

atari-ch05-exo-pset.enonce: The PSET routine from the manual (module 7.2) should draw the pixel (37, 10) in color 5. It assembles and does not crash, but the pixel does not appear: find and fix its two errors.
indices: Step through PSET and compare A0 with the computation in the lesson.
Look at A0 after `ADDA.L D0,A0`: what did the high word of D0 hold?
(X ÷ 16) × 8 is not X ÷ 2: you must align on 8 bytes (`$FFF8`), not on 2, and add only the low word of D0 (`ADDA.W`).
atari-ch05-exo-pset.source: PSET routine from the Atari ST manual v2, module 7.2, reproduced with its errors

atari-ch05-cours-palette.source: Rephrased from the Atari ST manual v1 (§ 3.4) and the "low-level graphics" sheet of v0.1

atari-ch05-ex-palette.titre: Changing the whole screen without redrawing it
atari-ch05-ex-palette.introduction: The program fills the screen with color no. 2, green by default, then changes only the palette; step through one or two rounds of the loop, then use Run to the end for the 4,000 rounds.

explications.6: 32,000 bytes make 4,000 groups of 8 bytes, and DBRA will go round 3,999 + 1 times.
explications.8: Plane 0 of the group receives 16 bits at 0.
explications.10: A long word at 0 fills planes 2 and 3 in one go, and the 16 pixels of the group have color %0010 = 2.
explications.11: The loop moves on to the next group, and the top of the screen fills with green.
explications.15: `Setcolor(2, $007)` makes color 2 blue, and the whole screen changes color at once without a single one of its bytes being modified.

atari-ch05-ex-palette.conclusion: Filling the screen takes 16,000 instructions, whereas a single call to Setcolor is enough to change its color.

atari-ch05-pred-palette.introduction: The program fills the screen in color 2, then calls Setcolor with another value.

q1.enonce: What color is the screen at the end?
q1.explication: The pixels carry number 2, and Setcolor has put $700, red, into color 2.

q2.enonce: How many bytes of screen memory did the Setcolor modify?
q2.explication: Setcolor changes only one palette register, not the screen memory.

atari-ch05-exo-rouge15.enonce: Give color 15 the value bright red (`$700`) with Setcolor.
indices: Push the color, then the number 15, then the function 7.
Three words pushed: 6 bytes to clean up.

atari-ch05-exo-remplir.enonce: Fill the whole screen with color 15 (`%1111`).
indices: Color 15 sets every bit of every plane to 1.
32,000 bytes make 8,000 long words: `MOVE.L #-1,(A0)+` in a loop of 7,999 + 1 rounds.

atari-ch05-bonus-carre.enonce: At the top left of the screen, draw a filled square of 16 × 16 pixels in color 4.
indices: A group is 16 pixels wide: one word per line, in the right plane, is enough.
Color 4, `%0100`, is in plane 2, at offset 4 of the group; the next line is 160 bytes further on.

q1.enonce: How many bytes does the ST screen take up?
q1.explication: 320 × 200 pixels of 4 bits make 32,000 bytes, as in medium and high resolution.

q2.enonce: In low resolution, how many bytes is a line?
q2.explication: A line holds 20 groups of 16 pixels, 8 bytes each.

q3.enonce: In a word of a plane, which bit matches the leftmost pixel?
q3.explication: The most significant bit matches the leftmost pixel.

q10.enonce: After a `TRAP #14`, which of these registers has certainly kept its value?
q10.explication: TOS preserves D3-D7 and A3-A6, but may modify D0-D2 and A0-A2; D0 receives its return value, besides.

q4.enonce: A pixel of color 6 (`%0110`) has its bit at 1 in planes…

q5.enonce: Which expression gives the offset of the group that holds pixel X?
q5.explication: You first divide by 16 in integer division, then multiply by 8; X ÷ 2 is only right when X is a multiple of 16.

q6.enonce: How many different colors can an ST (STF) produce?
q6.explication: With 3 bits per component, it produces 8 × 8 × 8 = 512 colors, 16 of them on screen; 4,096 is the STE.

q7.enonce: Which color does the palette value `$770` give?
q7.explication: Red at 7, green at 7 and blue at 0 give yellow.

q8.enonce: Why is changing the palette so fast?
choix: Because the Shifter redraws the screen by itself
Because you modify a single register instead of thousands of bytes
Because the palette is in ROM
q8.explication: All the pixels with the same number change color at the same time.

q11.enonce: Which instruction inverts every bit of D6.W, to build an inverted mask?
q11.explication: `NOT` inverts each bit, whereas `NEG` computes 0 − D6 and `EXT` extends the sign.

q9.enonce: On a 1040 STF, you write `$0FFF` into a color register, then read it back. What do you read?
q9.explication: The ST's Shifter keeps only 3 bits per component, in the format `0RRR0GGG0BBB`, so the extra bits are lost and you read back `$0777`; the STE keeps 4.
